## MotifbreakR Analysis : NPC MPRA

This document shows the preliminary motifbreakR analysis conducted on the significant SNPs found the in RenCell VM NPC MPRA.

#### Aim:

This quarto document identifies which of the NPC MPRA validated SNPs might have functional consequences by disrupting or creating transcription factor binding sites - potentially affecting gene regulation. This is a useful *in silico* follow up tool for interrogating the effectiveness of the MPRA chosen SNPs and prioritisation for further downstrema analysis.

```{r}
#load libraries
library(motifbreakR)
library(tidyverse)
library(BSgenome)
library("SNPlocs.Hsapiens.dbSNP155.GRCh38") # dbSNP155 in hg19
library("BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38")
library(MotifDb)
library(Cairo)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(DT)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

We first load the SNP files

-   Reads a file containing SNP identifiers (likely rsIDs like rs123456)
-   Converts them to a character vector
-   The `eval(parse())` is unusual here - it's parsing and evaluating the strings (possibly to handle special formatting)

```{r snps}
#load SNP file list
all_SNPs_file <- system.file("SNPs", package = "motifbreakR")
all_SNPs_file <- "C:/Users/chano/Bioinformatics/250912_motifbreakR_NPC/SNPs"
all_snps <- read.table(all_SNPs_file, header = TRUE)
all_snps <- as.character(all_snps) #ensure eveyrthing is a character vector
all_snps <- eval(parse(text = all_snps)) #for the weird spacing issues for formatting
all_snps


```

## Getting SNP genomic coordinates

We first check them from the 144 version from the dbSNP database. The newer version does not seem to load unfortunately and the genomic build is hg19

This provides a GRanges object for the SNPs we are interested in

```{r snpsmb}
snps.mb <- snps.from.rsid(rsid = all_snps,
                          dbSNP = SNPlocs.Hsapiens.dbSNP155.GRCh38,
                          search.genome = BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38)
as.data.frame(snps.mb) %>%
  datatable(
    caption = "Interactive SNP Browser",
    filter = 'top',
    options = list(
      pageLength = 10,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      autoWidth = TRUE
    )
  )


#Also view as ggplot 
as.data.frame(snps.mb) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = seqnames)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "SNP Distribution Across Chromosomes",
    x = "Chromosome",
    y = "Number of SNPs"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Finding broken motifs

Load and find broken motifs. We use HOCOMOCO for this.

The motifDb database is a R package which is an annotated collection of Protein-DNA Binding Sequence Motifs. Link attached here <https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MotifDb.html>. FOr people with no Chip-seq data this is a very valuable tool.

**HOCOMOCO** is a comprehensive collection of human transcription factor binding motifs (position weight matrices/PWMs). It represents a preferable binding spots for TFs. So if our SNPs are within those regions we would be able to see this. <https://hocomoco11.autosome.org/>

```{r motifDB}
#MotifDb
#table(mcols(MotifDb)$organism, mcols(MotifDb)$dataSource)
### Here we can see which organisms are availible under which sources
### in MotifDb

```

We have leveraged the `MotifList` introduced by [*MotifDb*](https://bioconductor.org/packages/3.22/MotifDb) to include an additional set of motifs that have been gathered to this package:

```{r motif}
data(motifbreakR_motif) #motiflist
#motifbreakR_motif
```

```{r hocomoco}
data(hocomoco)
#hocomoco
```

Now that we have the three necessary components to run [*motifbreakR*](https://bioconductor.org/packages/3.22/motifbreakR):

1.  A `BSgenome` object for our organism, in this case `BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19`

2.  A `MotifList` object containing our motifs, in this case `hocomoco`,

3.  And our input `GRanges` object generated by `snps.from.rsid`, in this case `snps.mb`

## Final Analysis

The final analysis is as follows. Core parameters are defined below.

-   **snpList**: Your SNPs with genomic coordinates
-   **filterp = TRUE**: Only report results that pass the p-value threshold
-   **pwmList = hocomoco**: Use HOCOMOCO motifs to test against
-   **threshold = 1e-4**: Significance threshold (p \< 0.0001)
-   **method = "ic"**: Uses "information content" scoring to assess motif disruption
-   **bkg**: Background nucleotide frequencies (assumes equal 25% for A, C, G, T)
-   **BPPARAM**: Run serially (not in parallel) - better for windows because only SerialParam worked for me

```{r results}
results_hocomoco <- motifbreakR(snpList = snps.mb, filterp = TRUE,
                       pwmList = hocomoco,
                       threshold = 1e-4, #can change this stringency
                       method = "ic",
                       bkg = c(A=0.25, C=0.25, G=0.25, T=0.25),
                       BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam()) #use this insteam to suit linunx like systemns

as.data.frame(results_hocomoco, row.names = NULL) %>%
  datatable(
    caption = "Transcription Factor Binding Sites Affected by SNPs",
    filter = 'top',
    options = list(
      pageLength = 15,
      scrollX = TRUE
    )
  )

```

```{r}
neg_genes <- unique(mcols(results_hocomoco)$geneSymbol[mcols(results_hocomoco)$alleleDiff < 0])
pos_genes <- unique(mcols(results_hocomoco)$geneSymbol[mcols(results_hocomoco)$alleleDiff > 0])

both_directions <- intersect(neg_genes, pos_genes)
length(both_directions)
```

The top 30 TFs affected due to motif disruptions from SNPs are shown below.

#### Basic overview of what this does

-   For each SNP, extracts the surrounding DNA sequence (reference and alternate alleles)
-   Scans both sequences against all transcription factor motifs in HOCOMOCO
-   Calculates binding scores for reference vs. alternate alleles
-   Identifies which SNPs **break** (disrupt) or **create** transcription factor binding sites

```{r snpid}
unique(mcols(results_hocomoco)$SNP_id) #Counts how many unique SNPs showed significant effects on transcription factor binding
unique(results_hocomoco$SNP_id) #list of unique SNPs. No duplications
unique(results_hocomoco$geneSymbol) #list of unique TFs. No duplications

```

To summarise,

```{r}
# Count unique SNPs
num_snps <- length(unique(mcols(results_hocomoco)$SNP_id))

# Count unique transcription factors
num_tfs <- length(unique(mcols(results_hocomoco)$geneSymbol))

# ANSI codes for bold and larger appearance (works in most R consoles)
bold_start <- "\033[1m"
bold_end <- "\033[0m"

# Print styled summary
cat(paste0("1. There are ", bold_start, num_snps, bold_end, " unique SNPs that disrupt transcription factor binding.\n"))
cat(paste0("2. There are ", bold_start, num_tfs, bold_end, " unique transcription factors with disrupted binding.\n"))

# Create frequency table
tf_freq_table <- as.data.frame(table(mcols(results_hocomoco)$geneSymbol)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Freq))

# Display frequency table using kable
kable(tf_freq_table, col.names = c("Transcription Factor", "Frequency"), caption = "Frequency of TF Motif Disruptions")

```

```{r}
# Step 1: Extract metadata safely
results_df <- as.data.frame(mcols(results_hocomoco))

# Step 2: Select relevant columns and remove duplicates
snp_tf_table <- results_df %>%
  select(SNP_id, geneSymbol) %>%
  distinct()

# Step 3: Group by SNP and collapse TFs into one line
snp_tf_summary <- snp_tf_table %>%
  group_by(SNP_id) %>%
  summarise(Disrupted_TFs = paste(unique(geneSymbol), collapse = ", ")) %>%
  arrange(SNP_id)

# Step 4: Display as a kable table
kable(snp_tf_summary, col.names = c("SNP (rsID)", "Disrupted Transcription Factors"), caption = "SNPs and Their Disrupted TFs")

```

## Motif Disruption graphs

All motifbreakR generated graphs are as follows.

**A bit of helpful information ; Letter Height = Information Content**

The height of each letter is proportional to:

```         
Letter height = Frequency × Information content
```

So:

-   **Big letter** = common AND important = high conservation

-   **Small letter** = rare OR unimportant = low conservation

    | Bits  | Meaning             | SNP Impact          |
    |-------|---------------------|---------------------|
    | \~2.0 | Always this base    | **STRONG**          |
    | \~1.5 | Strong preference   | **Moderate-Strong** |
    | \~1.0 | Moderate preference | **Moderate**        |
    | \~0.5 | Weak preference     | **Weak**            |
    | \~0.0 | No preference       | **Minimal**         |

```{r}
for (id in unique(mcols(results_hocomoco)$SNP_id)) {
  try({
    plotMB(results = results_hocomoco, rsid = id, effect = "strong")
    title(main = id)
  }, silent = TRUE)
}


```

## Further interrogation of transcription factors

To assess transcription factor enrichment for GO processes, I then did a pathway enrichment analysis using ShinyGO 0.85. I did this two ways.

1.  Background as all human transcription factors
2.  Background as all genes expressed in RenCell VM NPCs

### Method 1 : Background as all human transciption factors

A total of 91 unique transcritpion factors impacted in this subset of SNPs were used as input . Background SNPs were found from the link here <https://humantfs.ccbr.utoronto.ca/download.php> which highlights all human TFs from Lambert et al. (PMID 29425488) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29425488/>. I did not get the ideal enrichment of pathways I was hoping for
